sections.heading: Asking you to show me the truth about myself
sections.text: Father, you know me all the way down. When you let me see myself honestly, even for a moment, that is a mercy. I do not naturally enjoy it, but I need it. My sin is the worst thing about me, and you are the best thing I have. Keep me from defending myself, polishing my image, or trying to make my own mess look respectable. No one should brag about a manure pile.
theological_themes: God searches the heart and graciously exposes what is hidden.
True self-knowledge leads to humility, not self-hatred as an end in itself.
Sin is the believer’s deepest evil, and God himself is the believer’s greatest good.

scripture_references.connection: David asks God to search him and expose any grievous way in him, trusting God’s knowledge as a mercy that leads him back onto the right path.
Paul’s confession about the weakness of his flesh gives biblical shape to the prayer’s refusal to flatter the self or treat sin as a small problem.

sections.heading: Owning the harm my sin does
sections.text: Lord, help me stop pretending that my sin stays private and contained. My family, my church, and even the places where I live are affected by the ways I disobey you. When I treat sin as small, I lie about you and about myself. Teach me to believe what you say: sin is serious, and your anger against evil is not imaginary.
theological_themes: Personal sin can damage households, churches, and communities.
Minimizing sin is spiritually dangerous because it denies God’s holiness and moral judgment.
Repentance includes taking responsibility for the real effects of sin.

scripture_references.connection: Paul warns the church that tolerated sin spreads through the whole community like leaven, showing that sin is never merely a private matter.
This passage grounds the prayer’s claim that God is truly opposed to evil; divine wrath is not a human exaggeration but God’s settled righteousness against ungodliness.

sections.heading: Refusing to measure myself by other people
sections.text: Do not let me use decent, respected Christians as the final measuring stick for my life. Even the best people are still unfinished. They are not always steady, not always holy, not always joyful in suffering, and not always as faithful as you call them to be. Keep my eyes on you and on your Word, not on comparisons that make me feel safer than I really am.
theological_themes: Human examples can help but cannot replace God’s standard.
Holiness is measured by God’s character and will, not by relative human respectability.

scripture_references.connection: Paul exposes the foolishness of self-measurement by comparison with others, which fits the prayer’s concern that looking sideways can produce false confidence.
Peter calls believers to holiness because God is holy, making God’s character—not the average conduct of other believers—the standard.

sections.heading: Learning to discern what looks acceptable but comes from wrong motives
sections.text: Give me a clearer conscience and better judgment. Show me when something I call good is actually evil. Show me when something may be technically allowed, but in me it grows out of a corrupt root—wanting to be admired, wanting power, wanting money, or finding a respectable way to use people for my own gain. I do not trust myself to see this without your help.
theological_themes: Moral discernment includes motives, not only outward legality.
A lawful action can become sinful when driven by pride, greed, or self-interest.
God’s wisdom is needed because the heart can misread itself.

scripture_references.connection: This proverb teaches that people often consider their own ways pure while the Lord weighs the spirit behind them, directly supporting the prayer’s concern with hidden motives.
Paul distinguishes what is lawful from what is helpful or loving, showing that Christian ethics cannot stop at bare permission.
Paul warns that the desire to be rich can lead people into ruin, which bears on the prayer’s concern about wealth-seeking that looks acceptable but springs from evil desire.

sections.heading: Remembering what I lack and asking for grace
sections.text: Please keep my neediness in front of me. I need to know your will from Scripture better than I do. I need wisdom when others look to me for help. I need daily repentance, because when I avoid turning back to you, I push away the nearness I most need. I need real prayer—not just words, but words with love and faith in them. I need zeal for your glory instead of always bending things toward my own purposes. I need joy in you and in what you want. I need love for other people that is not thin, selective, or mainly convenient for me. Give me grace for all of this.
theological_themes: The Christian life depends on grace for Scripture-shaped wisdom, repentance, prayer, zeal, joy, and love.
Lack of repentance cools fellowship with God, though grace remains the source of return.
Prayer without love and faith can become empty words.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that Scripture equips God’s people for every good work, grounding the prayer’s request to know God’s will through the Bible.
James invites believers who lack wisdom to ask God, which supports the prayer’s request for wisdom in guiding and helping others.
John connects confession with God’s faithful forgiveness and cleansing, giving biblical shape to the need for ongoing repentance.
Paul warns that impressive spiritual speech and action are empty without love, fitting the prayer’s concern about having words in prayer without love.

sections.heading: Drawing from the true fountain, not stopping short
sections.text: Father, do not let me set up my life so close to living water and still never drink. Do not let me run a pipe that stops just short of the spring—near the truth, near prayer, near the church, near the promises, but not actually receiving life from you. Bring me all the way to yourself. Let me draw from the deep water you give from above, through Christ and by your Spirit.
theological_themes: Religious nearness is not the same as living communion with God.
God himself is the fountain of life, and believers must actually receive from him.
The Spirit gives the living water Christ promises.

scripture_references.connection: God rebukes his people for forsaking him, the fountain of living waters, which closely illuminates the image of stopping short of the true source.

Jesus invites the thirsty to come to him and drink, and John connects this living water with the Spirit, supporting the prayer’s plea to receive life from God rather than merely remain near religious things.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original says the speaker’s sins make his country, family, and church fare worse and can bring judgment. I preserved the corporate seriousness of sin while avoiding a simplistic claim that every hardship in those spheres is a direct punishment for one person’s sin.

The reference to gaining wealth “by usury” is historically and ethically complex, since Christian traditions have differed on whether all interest, exploitative lending, or greed-driven lending is in view. I rendered it more broadly as respectable-looking financial self-interest that uses people for gain.

The original’s language of self-loathing is severe. I kept its penitential force—refusing self-honor and self-flattery—while avoiding language that could imply hatred of oneself as a created person made in God’s image.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “a glimpse of myself” as God-given honest self-knowledge, not morbid introspection.
I took “good men” to mean respected believers whose example can be helpful but must not become the final moral standard.
I understood “lawful comes from an evil principle” as the difference between outward permission and inward motive, so the modern prayer names reputation, power, money, and using others as examples.
I rendered the final image of the pipe falling short of the fountain as being near religious means—truth, prayer, church, promises—without actually drawing life from God.
